data.title: Tinea pedis & onychomycosis — viva
data.summary: Fungal infections · 12 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Tinea pedis & onychomycosis** (Fungal infections)_

**Q1. Clinical types of tinea pedis.**
- Interdigital (commonest; 4th web space; maceration, fissuring, scaling) — dermatophyte complex with bacteria (Gram-negative 'dermatophytosis complex')
- Moccasin (chronic hyperkeratotic, T. rubrum; diffuse fine scaling of soles and sides)
- Vesiculobullous (inflammatory, instep, T. mentagrophytes/interdigitale)
- Acute ulcerative (Gram-negative superinfection)
- 'Two feet, one hand' syndrome — tinea pedis with tinea manuum of one hand

**Q2. Risk factors for tinea pedis.**
- Occlusive footwear, sweating, communal bathing/swimming pools, sports, diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, immunosuppression

**Q3. Differential diagnosis of tinea pedis.**
- Interdigital: erythrasma (coral-red), candidal intertrigo, Gram-negative infection, soft corn
- Plantar: psoriasis, keratoderma, contact dermatitis (dorsum), dyshidrotic eczema, juvenile plantar dermatosis, pitted keratolysis

**Q4. Define onychomycosis. Organisms?**
- Fungal infection of the nail unit — dermatophytes (tinea unguium; T. rubrum, T. interdigitale) ~ 70–90% in toenails, non-dermatophyte moulds (Scopulariopsis, Fusarium, Aspergillus, Neoscytalidium) and Candida (fingernails, chronic paronychia)

**Q5. Classify onychomycosis by clinical pattern (PYQ).**
- Distal lateral subungual (DLSO) — commonest; invasion via hyponychium; subungual hyperkeratosis, onycholysis, yellow discolouration
- Proximal subungual (PSO) — through proximal nail fold; white under proximal nail; marker of HIV/immunosuppression (T. rubrum) or moulds (Fusarium with paronychia)
- Superficial white (SWO) — chalky white patches on the nail surface (T. interdigitale, moulds); superficial black variant
- Endonyx — milky white nail without hyperkeratosis (T. soudanense, T. violaceum)
- Total dystrophic — end stage
- Mixed patterns; Candida onychomycosis (with chronic paronychia; CMC — total dystrophy)
- Dermatophytoma — yellow/white longitudinal streak or patch (fungal ball) — poor response

**Q6. How do you sample a nail for diagnosis?**
- Clean with alcohol; take subungual debris from the most proximal part of the affected area (DLSO), scrape the surface (SWO), punch/drill proximal plate (PSO)
- KOH 20–40% (± DMSO), wait or warm; culture on SDA with and without cycloheximide (moulds need the latter)
- Nail clipping histology with PAS — most sensitive single test
- PCR; dermoscopy (spiked/jagged proximal border of onycholysis, longitudinal streaks, 'aurora borealis' pattern)
- Non-dermatophyte mould is accepted as cause only when repeatedly isolated / seen in direct microscopy

**Q7. Differential diagnosis of nail dystrophy.**
- Nail psoriasis (pits, oil-drop sign, onycholysis with red border, salmon patch), lichen planus (pterygium, thinning), traumatic onychodystrophy (shoe pressure), yellow nail syndrome, onychogryphosis, eczema, subungual tumours (SCC, melanoma), pachyonychia congenita, Darier's disease

**Q8. Systemic treatment of onychomycosis.**
- Terbinafine 250 mg/day — 6 weeks fingernails, 12 weeks toenails (drug of choice for dermatophyte)
- Itraconazole pulse: 200 mg twice daily for 1 week every month — 2 pulses fingernails, 3–4 toenails (also covers Candida and some moulds); or continuous 200 mg/day
- Fluconazole 150–450 mg once weekly for 6–12 months (fingernails 6, toenails 9–12)
- Efficacy assessed at 12–18 months as nail grows out (toenail grows ~1 mm/month)

**Q9. Topical treatment of onychomycosis.**
- For mild DLSO (<50% nail, no matrix involvement), SWO, children, or with oral therapy
- Amorolfine 5% lacquer weekly; ciclopirox 8% lacquer daily; efinaconazole 10% solution; tavaborole 5% (US approvals)
- Adjuncts: nail avulsion (chemical with 40% urea or surgical), debridement, laser and photodynamic therapy (limited evidence)

**Q10. What are the poor prognostic factors?**
- Matrix involvement, >50% nail affected, dermatophytoma, lateral edge disease, thick nail plate (>2 mm), slow growth, elderly, diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, immunosuppression, non-dermatophyte moulds

**Q11. What is Scytalidium/Neoscytalidium infection?**
- Non-dermatophyte mould causing moccasin-like tinea and onychomycosis in tropics; resistant to most antifungals; cycloheximide sensitive (grows only on media without it)

**Q12. Prevention of recurrence?**
- Treat tinea pedis, dry feet and web spaces, antifungal powder in shoes, change socks, avoid barefoot in communal areas, discard old footwear, treat family members, periodic topical (amorolfine) use

## Quick spotter facts
- Proximal white subungual onychomycosis — screen for HIV
- Terbinafine 6 weeks fingernail / 12 weeks toenail
- Dermatophytoma — streak in nail, needs removal + oral therapy

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Superficial fungal infections, nail infections). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
